steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction for a paper proposing curvature regularization (curvNLOS) for non-line-of-sight imaging from under-sampled measurements. Cover NLOS imaging and its applications, existing reconstruction methods, ways to speed up acquisition, why curvature regularization fits, and our contributions.

steps.name: skeleton_outline
steps.text:
- NLOS imaging: what it is, applications, recent advances
- Reconstruction methods: direct, iterative, deep learning
- Reducing acquisition time: multi-pixel systems and fewer scanning points
- Under-sampled data and curvature regularization
- Our work (curvNLOS) and contributions

steps.name: detailed_outline
steps.text:
- NLOS imaging
  - time-resolved measurements -> recover 3D shape and appearance of hidden objects beyond line of sight
  - applications: autonomous driving, 3D human pose estimation, sensor system, others
  - advances in single-photon detectors and large-scale inverse problem algorithms
  - examples: imaging over 1.43 km; tracking at resolution 0.6 mm at 0.55 m
- Reconstruction methods
  - inverse problem very challenging
  - three categories: direct, iterative, deep learning-based
  - filtered back-projection: fast direct method; filter data, back-project (paint data back along measurement direction)
  - other direct: phasor field, frequency-domain method, Fermat flow; model physical imaging process
  - direct: fast, efficient, sensitive to noise and measurement distortions
  - iterative: priors regularize problem, better image quality; much more computational time
  - deep learning: CNN models; depend on training datasets; may lose impact on real measurement data and spatial/temporal degradation data
- Reducing acquisition time
  - dense raster scanning bad for high-speed NLOS
  - strategy 1, multi-pixel time-of-flight systems: Nam et al. SPAD array detectors + fast reconstruction -> live low-latency videos; Pei et al. SPAD array + optimization-based method, 20 frames per second
  - strategy 2, fewer scanning points: Isogawa et al. circular and confocal scan (points on a circle on visible wall, lower-dimensional transients); Ye et al. compressed sensing in active NLOS; Zhang et al. Archimedean spiral scanning for confocal NLOS, much less acquisition time
- Under-sampled data and curvature regularization
  - under-sampled measurements -> high-speed acquisition, but image degradation
  - regularization methods: sparse, surface area, curvature
  - curvature: models continuities of edges and surfaces
  - first used in image inpainting (results meeting human perception)
  - then surface reconstruction, sparse image reconstruction
  - captures tiny elongated structures -> image segmentation, tubular structure tracking
  - good choice for under-sampled NLOS: smooth reconstructed surfaces
- Our work
  - curvNLOS: curvature regularization model for under-sampled NLOS; good surfaces from few measurements
  - ADMM-based numerical algorithm, GPU computation
  - experiments on synthetic and real data; smoothness of object and estimated signals
  - contributions: curvature models (smooth surfaces, fill sparse signals); fast iterative algorithms (high-order curvature as adaptive TV weight, linearization, GPU-friendly); GPU-based NLOS package; comparison with state of the art on confocal and non-confocal settings, robust with under-sampled data

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
Non-line-of-sight (NLOS) imaging uses time-resolved measurements to recover the 3D shape and the visual appearance of hidden objects that are beyond the direct line of sight of the sensors. It has many applications, like autonomous driving, 3D human pose estimation, sensor system, and many other domains. Recent advances in single-photon detector technology and in computational algorithms for large-scale inverse problems make NLOS imaging feasible in different conditions. For example, NLOS imaging has been demonstrated over a distance of 1.43 km, and real-time tracking of hidden objects at a resolution of 0.6 mm at a distance of 0.55 m.

Reconstructing the 3D shape and appearance of the hidden object is an inverse problem that is also very challenging. Roughly, the NLOS reconstruction methods can be put into three categories: direct reconstruction methods, iterative reconstruction methods, and deep learning-based reconstruction methods. The filtered back-projection algorithm is a fast direct method, it filters the data and does the back-projection operation, where the data is painted back in the image along the direction in which it is measured. Other direct reconstruction methods include the phasor field, the frequency-domain method, the Fermat flow method, etc, which are proposed by modeling the physical process of imaging. The direct methods are fast and efficient, but they are sensitive to noises and measurement distortions. Iterative reconstruction methods introduce priors to regularize the NLOS reconstruction problem and improve image quality. They can give high-quality reconstruction images, but they take much more computational time than direct methods. With the development of deep learning, convolutional neural network models have also been developed for the NLOS reconstruction problem. But deep learning methods depend a lot on the training datasets, so they may lose their impact on real measurement data and on spatial/temporal degradation data.

The dense raster scanning that these methods use is bad for high-speed NLOS applications. So different strategies have been used to reduce the acquisition time. One strategy is to use a multi-pixel time-of-flight NLOS system. Nam et al. used specially designed single photon avalanche diode (SPAD) array detectors to get a multi-pixel NLOS imaging method, together with a fast reconstruction algorithm that can capture and reconstruct live low-latency videos of NLOS scenes. Pei et al. used the SPAD array and an optimization-based computational method and got NLOS reconstruction at 20 frames per second. Another strategy is to reconstruct the scene with fewer scanning points. Isogawa et al. proposed a circular and confocal non-line-of-sight scan, where the sampling points form a circle on a visible wall, which reduces the dimension of the transient measurements. Ye et al. explored compressed sensing in active NLOS imaging to reduce how many scanning points are needed, for fast implementation. Zhang et al. proposed an Archimedean spiral scanning method based on confocal non-line-of-sight imaging, which reduces the data acquisition time a lot.

- under-sampled data: previous works show reconstruction from under-sampled measurements for fast acquisition, but sparse measurements degrade images; regularization: sparse, surface area, curvature; curvature models continuities of edges and surfaces; first image inpainting, then surface reconstruction, sparse image reconstruction; tiny elongated structures -> segmentation, tubular structure tracking; good choice for smooth NLOS surfaces
- our work: curvNLOS for under-sampled NLOS, good surfaces from few measurements; ADMM-based algorithm on GPU; synthetic + real data experiments; smoothness of object and estimated signals
- contributions:
  - curvature regularization models: restore smooth hidden surfaces, fill in sparse signals
  - fast iterative algorithms: high-order curvature as adaptive weight for total variation, linearization -> GPU-friendly
  - GPU-based NLOS reconstruction package for high-speed applications
  - vs state of the art: robust on confocal and non-confocal settings, especially under-sampled data

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
Non-line-of-sight (NLOS) imaging uses time-resolved measurements to recover the 3D shape and the visual appearance of hidden objects that are beyond the direct line of sight of the sensors. It has many applications, like autonomous driving, 3D human pose estimation, sensor system, and many other domains. Recent advances in single-photon detector technology and in computational algorithms for large-scale inverse problems make NLOS imaging feasible in different conditions. For example, NLOS imaging has been demonstrated over a distance of 1.43 km, and real-time tracking of hidden objects at a resolution of 0.6 mm at a distance of 0.55 m.

Reconstructing the 3D shape and appearance of the hidden object is an inverse problem that is also very challenging. Roughly, the NLOS reconstruction methods can be put into three categories: direct reconstruction methods, iterative reconstruction methods, and deep learning-based reconstruction methods. The filtered back-projection algorithm is a fast direct method, it filters the data and does the back-projection operation, where the data is painted back in the image along the direction in which it is measured. Other direct reconstruction methods include the phasor field, the frequency-domain method, the Fermat flow method, etc, which are proposed by modeling the physical process of imaging. The direct methods are fast and efficient, but they are sensitive to noises and measurement distortions. Iterative reconstruction methods introduce priors to regularize the NLOS reconstruction problem and improve image quality. They can give high-quality reconstruction images, but they take much more computational time than direct methods. With the development of deep learning, convolutional neural network models have also been developed for the NLOS reconstruction problem. But deep learning methods depend a lot on the training datasets, so they may lose their impact on real measurement data and on spatial/temporal degradation data.

The dense raster scanning that these methods use is bad for high-speed NLOS applications. So different strategies have been used to reduce the acquisition time. One strategy is to use a multi-pixel time-of-flight NLOS system. Nam et al. used specially designed single photon avalanche diode (SPAD) array detectors to get a multi-pixel NLOS imaging method, together with a fast reconstruction algorithm that can capture and reconstruct live low-latency videos of NLOS scenes. Pei et al. used the SPAD array and an optimization-based computational method and got NLOS reconstruction at 20 frames per second. Another strategy is to reconstruct the scene with fewer scanning points. Isogawa et al. proposed a circular and confocal non-line-of-sight scan, where the sampling points form a circle on a visible wall, which reduces the dimension of the transient measurements. Ye et al. explored compressed sensing in active NLOS imaging to reduce how many scanning points are needed, for fast implementation. Zhang et al. proposed an Archimedean spiral scanning method based on confocal non-line-of-sight imaging, which reduces the data acquisition time a lot.

As previous works show, NLOS reconstruction can be done with under-sampled measurements so that acquisition is fast. But sparse measurements may degrade the reconstructed images. Effective regularization methods have been used for many shape and image processing tasks, like sparse regularization, surface area regularization, and curvature regularization, etc. Curvature regularization is well-known among them for being able to model the continuities of edges and surfaces. It was first applied to image inpainting, to restore results that satisfy human perception. Because it is good at recovering missing data, curvature regularity has also been used for surface reconstruction and sparse image reconstruction. And since curvature regularization can capture tiny but elongated structures in images, it has been used for image segmentation, tubular structure tracking, etc. So curvature regularization is a good choice for under-sampled NLOS imaging problems to get smooth and satisfying reconstructed surfaces.

In this paper we study a curvature regularization reconstruction model for under-sampled NLOS imaging problems, which we call curvNLOS, and which can reconstruct good quality surfaces from as few measurements as possible. We also develop an effective numerical algorithm based on the alternating direction methods of multipliers (ADMM), which can be solved with GPU computation. We do comprehensive experiments on synthetic and real data. The numerical results show that curvature regularization can effectively guarantee that the object and the estimated signals are smooth. The main contributions of this work are:

- • We propose new curvature regularization models for the NLOS imaging problem, where the curvature regularization is used to restore the smooth surface of hidden objects and to fill in the sparse measured signals.

- • We present fast iterative optimization algorithms for the curvature minimization problems, where the high-order curvature is used as the adaptive weight for total variation, and a linearization technique gives GPU-friendly iterative algorithms.

- • We develop a GPU-based NLOS reconstruction package that uses the parallel computation ability of GPUs, which is what high-speed NLOS applications need.

- • Compared with the state-of-the-art NLOS methods, our curvature regularization models can robustly restore the estimated signals and the three-dimensional scene points in both confocal and non-confocal settings, especially when the measured data is under-sampled.

steps.text:
Non-line-of-sight (NLOS) imaging uses time-resolved measurements to recover the 3D shape and visual appearance of hidden objects beyond the direct line of sight of sensors [1,2], with various applications such as autonomous driving [3], 3D human pose estimation [4], sensor system [5,6], and many other domains. Recent advances in single-photon detector technology and in computational algorithms for solving large-scale inverse problems make NLOS imaging feasible in different conditions. For instance, NLOS imaging and real-time tracking of hidden objects have been demonstrated over a distance of 1.43 km [7] and at a resolution of 0.6 mm at a distance of 0.55 m [8,9], respectively.

The inverse problem of reconstructing the 3D shape and appearance of the hidden object is also very challenging [10,11]. Roughly speaking, NLOS imaging reconstruction methods can be divided into three categories: direct reconstruction methods, iterative reconstruction methods, and deep learning-based reconstruction methods. The filtered back-projection algorithm is a fast direct method that filters the data and performs the back-projection operation, where the data is painted back in the image along the direction it is measured [12,13,14]. Other direct reconstruction methods include the phasor field [15], the frequency-domain method [16], the Fermat flow method [17], etc., which are proposed by modeling the physical process of imaging. These direct methods are fast and efficient but sensitive to noises and measurement distortions. Iterative reconstruction methods introduce priors to regularize the NLOS reconstruction problem and improve the image quality [18,19,20,21,22]. Although they can provide high-quality reconstruction images, they also consume much more computational time than direct methods. With the development of deep learning, convolutional neural network models have been developed for solving the NLOS reconstruction problem [23,24,25,26,27]. However, deep learning methods are highly dependent on the training datasets, which may cause them to lose their impact on real measurement data and spatial/temporal degradation data [23].

Indeed, the dense raster scanning used in the aforementioned methods is detrimental to high-speed NLOS applications. Different strategies have therefore been employed to reduce the acquisition time. One strategy is to use a multi-pixel time-of-flight NLOS system. Nam et al. [28] used specifically designed single photon avalanche diode (SPAD) array detectors to realize a multi-pixel NLOS imaging method, together with a fast reconstruction algorithm that can capture and reconstruct live low-latency videos of NLOS scenes. Pei et al. [29] used the SPAD array and an optimization-based computational method to achieve NLOS reconstruction at 20 frames per second. Another strategy is to use fewer scanning points to reconstruct the scene. Isogawa et al. [30] proposed a circular and confocal non-line-of-sight scan, in which the sampling points form a circle on a visible wall to reduce the dimension of transient measurements. Ye et al. [21] explored compressed sensing in active NLOS imaging to reduce the required number of scanning points for fast implementation. Zhang et al. [31] proposed an Archimedean spiral scanning method based on confocal non-line-of-sight imaging, which greatly reduces the data acquisition time.

As illustrated in previous works [30,21], NLOS reconstruction can be realized from under-sampled measurements to facilitate high-speed acquisition. However, sparse measurements may lead to degradation of the reconstructed images. Effective regularization methods have been used for various shape and image processing tasks, such as sparse regularization [32], surface area regularization [33], and curvature regularization [34,35,36], etc. Among them, curvature regularization is well-known for its ability to model the continuities of edges and surfaces. Curvature regularization was initially applied to image inpainting to restore satisfactory results that meet human perception [37,38,39]. Due to its superiority in recovering missing data, curvature regularity has also been used for surface reconstruction [40,41] and sparse image reconstruction [42,43]. Since curvature regularization can capture tiny but elongated structures in images, it has also been used for image segmentation [44], tubular structure tracking [45], etc. Curvature regularization is thus a good choice for under-sampled NLOS imaging problems to obtain smooth and satisfying reconstructed surfaces.

In this paper, we study a curvature regularization reconstruction model for under-sampled NLOS imaging problems, called curvNLOS, which can reconstruct surfaces of good quality from as few measurements as possible. We also develop an effective numerical algorithm based on the alternating direction methods of multipliers (ADMM), which can be solved with GPU computation. Comprehensive experiments are conducted on both synthetic and real data. The numerical results demonstrate that curvature regularization can effectively guarantee the smoothness of the object and the estimated signals. The main contributions of this work can be summarized as follows:

- • We propose novel curvature regularization models for solving the NLOS imaging problem, where the curvature regularization is used to restore the smooth surface of hidden objects and fill in the sparse measured signals.

- • We present fast iterative optimization algorithms for solving the curvature minimization problems, where the high-order curvature is regarded as the adaptive weight for total variation, and a linearization technique is used to obtain GPU-friendly iterative algorithms.

- • We develop a GPU-based NLOS reconstruction package that utilizes the parallel computation ability of GPUs, which is desirable for high-speed NLOS applications.

- • Compared with state-of-the-art NLOS methods, our curvature regularization models can robustly restore estimated signals and three-dimensional scene points in both confocal and non-confocal settings, especially when the measured data are under-sampled.
